course.title: Welding and Metalwork
course.tagline: Cut, join and shape metal into gates, frames and furniture.

days.title: Welding Safety: Gear Up
days.goal: Know the safety gear and rules before you strike an arc.
steps: Wear a welding helmet, gloves, long sleeves and boots.
Learn that the arc (the bright light) can burn eyes and skin.
Work in fresh air: welding smoke is harmful to breathe.
Keep water and a fire extinguisher close.
days.task: Put on full safety gear and check every item.
days.challenge: Name every piece of safety gear and what it protects.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to put on before welding?
options: Full safety gear: helmet, gloves, long sleeves, boots
quiz.explain: Full gear protects eyes, skin and feet from arc light, sparks and hot metal.

quiz.q: Why is welding smoke dangerous?
options: It is harmful to breathe and needs fresh air
quiz.explain: Welding fumes carry metal particles that harm lungs, so work in fresh air.

quiz.q: What is the arc in welding?
options: The bright light and heat that melts the metal
quiz.explain: The arc is the electric spark that melts metal so pieces join.

days.title: Welding Tools and Metals
days.goal: Know the welder, rods and the metals you will join.
steps: Learn the parts: the welder, the electrode holder and the earth clamp.
A welding rod (electrode) is the stick that melts to join metal.
Feel mild steel, the easiest metal for beginners.
Set up a clean metal workbench.
days.task: Label the parts of a welder: holder, clamp and dials.
days.challenge: Tell mild steel from aluminium by look and weight.

days.title: Strike Your First Arc
days.goal: Strike an arc and hold it steady on scrap metal.
steps: Clamp the earth lead to your metal piece.
Tap the rod on the metal like striking a match to start the arc.
Hold the rod a few millimetres from the metal to keep the arc alive.
Practise striking the arc ten times in a row.
days.task: Strike and hold an arc for five seconds on scrap.
days.challenge: Strike the arc first try, five times in a row.

days.title: Stick Welding Basics
days.goal: Run your first straight weld beads on flat metal.
steps: A weld bead is the line of melted metal that joins two pieces.
Move the rod slowly and steadily along the joint.
Keep the same angle and distance the whole way.
Let the bead cool, then chip off the slag (the crust on top).
days.task: Run three straight beads on flat metal.
days.challenge: Run a bead that is straight and even from end to end.

quiz.q: What is a welding rod?
options: The stick that melts to join metal
quiz.explain: The rod (electrode) melts into the joint to form the weld.

quiz.q: What is a weld bead?
options: The line of melted metal that joins two pieces
quiz.explain: The bead is the raised line of metal left after welding.

quiz.q: What is slag?
options: The crust that forms on top of a stick weld
quiz.explain: Slag is the crust that covers a stick weld and must be chipped off.

days.title: Weld Beads: Straight and Even
days.goal: Practise beads until they are straight, even and strong.
steps: Watch the molten pool (the glowing liquid metal) and follow it.
Move at a steady speed: too fast makes a thin bead, too slow makes a fat one.
Keep the rod angle the same.
Compare your beads and keep the best one.
days.task: Run five beads and pick the straightest one.
days.challenge: Run a bead with no gaps or holes in it.

quiz.q: What is a welding rod?
options: The stick that melts to join metal
quiz.explain: The rod (electrode) melts into the joint to form the weld.

quiz.q: What is a weld bead?
options: The line of melted metal that joins two pieces
quiz.explain: The bead is the raised line of metal left after welding.

quiz.q: What is slag?
options: The crust that forms on top of a stick weld
quiz.explain: Slag is the crust that covers a stick weld and must be chipped off.

days.title: Join Two Pieces: Butt Joint
days.goal: Weld two flat pieces edge to edge.
steps: Line the two pieces up with a tiny gap between them.
Tack weld (small spot welds) at both ends to hold them.
Run a bead along the whole joint.
Check the back: the weld should show through.
days.task: Weld two plates edge to edge so they hold firm.
days.challenge: Weld a butt joint that does not break when bent.

quiz.q: What is a welding rod?
options: The stick that melts to join metal
quiz.explain: The rod (electrode) melts into the joint to form the weld.

quiz.q: What is a weld bead?

quiz.explain: The bead is the raised line of metal left after welding.

days.title: Project: Run Weld Beads on a Practice Plate
days.goal: Fill a practice plate with neat parallel beads.

video.title: How to Strike an Arc: Stick Welding Basics

steps: Clean the plate and clamp it flat.
Run beads in straight parallel lines across the plate.
Keep each bead the same width and spacing.
Chip the slag and inspect every bead.
days.task: Finish a plate covered in neat, even beads.
days.challenge: Fill the plate with beads that are all the same width.

quiz.q: How do you start an arc?
options: Tap the rod like striking a match
quiz.explain: A light tap like striking a match starts the arc.

quiz.q: How far should the rod sit from the metal?
quiz.explain: A small gap keeps the arc alive; touching it kills the arc.

quiz.q: What happens if you move the rod too fast?
options: The bead is thin and weak
quiz.explain: Moving too fast leaves too little metal, so the bead is thin and weak.

project.title: Run Weld Beads on a Practice Plate
project.brief: Fill a practice plate with neat parallel weld beads.

days.title: Tack Welding
days.goal: Use tack welds to hold pieces in place before the full weld.

video.title: How to Strike an Arc: Stick Welding Basics

steps: A tack weld is a small quick weld that holds parts together.
Tack at the ends and the middle of a joint.
Check the pieces are square before you tack.
Tack, check, then weld fully.
days.task: Tack a frame square before welding it fully.
days.challenge: Tack a frame so it stays square after welding.

days.title: Weld a Corner Joint
days.goal: Weld two pieces at a right angle.

video.title: How to Strike an Arc: Stick Welding Basics

steps: Set the pieces at 90 degrees and clamp them.
Tack both ends, then check the angle with a square.
Run a bead along the inside corner.
Check the joint is strong and square.
days.task: Weld a corner joint that is square and strong.
days.challenge: Weld a corner with no gaps at the ends.

days.title: Stick Welding (SMAW) 101
days.goal: Understand stick welding: rods, current and settings.
steps: SMAW is the full name for stick welding.
Learn that thicker rods need more current (power).
Set the welder to the right amps for your rod size.
Practise with the settings from the rod box.
days.task: Set a welder to the right amps for a rod size.
days.challenge: Explain what SMAW means in plain words.

quiz.q: What does SMAW stand for?
options: Shielded Metal Arc Welding, the full name for stick welding
quiz.explain: SMAW is stick welding: a rod shielded by its own coating.

quiz.q: What happens if the current is too high?
options: It burns holes in the metal
quiz.explain: Too much current melts through thin metal and leaves holes.

quiz.q: Why test settings on scrap first?
options: So the real piece is welded with the right settings
quiz.explain: Scrap lets you dial in the settings before touching the real work.

days.title: Rod Sizes and Current
days.goal: Pick the right rod and current for the metal thickness.
steps: Thin metal needs a thin rod and low current.
Thick metal needs a thick rod and higher current.
Too much current burns holes; too little makes a weak weld.
Test on scrap before you weld the real piece.
days.task: Pick the right rod and amps for three metal thicknesses.
days.challenge: Weld thin metal without burning a hole in it.

quiz.q: What does SMAW stand for?
options: Shielded Metal Arc Welding, the full name for stick welding
quiz.explain: SMAW is stick welding: a rod shielded by its own coating.

quiz.q: What happens if the current is too high?

days.title: Weld a Small Frame
days.goal: Weld four bars into a square frame.
steps: Cut four bars to size with a grinder or saw.
Tack the corners, check the frame is square.
Weld each corner fully.
Check the frame is flat and square.
days.task: Weld a square frame that is flat and true.
days.challenge: Weld a frame with all four corners square.

days.title: Stick Welding Practice
days.goal: Practise stick welding until your beads are neat.
steps: Run beads on flat, then on a corner joint.
Practise starting and stopping cleanly.
Chip slag and look for holes (porosity) in your beads.
Repeat your weakest bead until it improves.
days.task: Run ten beads and keep your three best.
days.challenge: Run a bead with no holes in it at all.

quiz.q: Why practise beads on flat metal first?
options: Flat beads teach speed, angle and distance before joints
quiz.explain: Flat practice builds the hand control every joint needs.

quiz.q: What are holes in a weld called?
quiz.explain: Porosity is tiny holes from gas trapped in the weld, often from dirty metal.

quiz.q: What causes porosity in a weld?
quiz.explain: Rust, paint and damp rods trap gas in the weld and leave holes.

days.goal: Weld a small frame for a table or stool.

Test the frame: it should hold weight without bending.
days.task: Finish a small welded frame, square and strong.
days.challenge: Build a frame that holds your weight.

days.title: MIG Welding Basics
days.goal: Learn MIG welding: wire feed, gas and settings.
steps: MIG welding feeds a wire through a gun while gas shields the weld.
Learn the parts: the gun, the wire spool and the gas bottle.
Set the wire speed and voltage for your metal thickness.
Practise on scrap before the real piece.
days.task: Set up a MIG welder and run a bead on scrap.
days.challenge: Explain how MIG is different from stick welding.

quiz.q: Why practise beads on flat metal first?
options: Flat beads teach speed, angle and distance before joints
quiz.explain: Flat practice builds the hand control every joint needs.

quiz.q: What are holes in a weld called?
quiz.explain: Porosity is tiny holes from gas trapped in the weld, often from dirty metal.

quiz.q: What causes porosity in a weld?
quiz.explain: Rust, paint and damp rods trap gas in the weld and leave holes.

days.title: MIG Beads on Flat Metal
days.goal: Run neat MIG beads on flat metal.
steps: Hold the gun at a steady angle and distance.
Pull the trigger and move at a steady speed.
Listen for a steady crackle: that is the sound of a good MIG weld.
Check the bead is even with no holes.
days.task: Run five neat MIG beads on flat metal.
days.challenge: Run a MIG bead that sounds like steady bacon frying.

quiz.q: How does MIG welding work?
options: A wire feeds through a gun while gas shields the weld
quiz.explain: MIG feeds wire automatically and shields the weld with gas.

quiz.q: What sound does a good MIG weld make?
options: A steady crackle like bacon frying
quiz.explain: A steady crackle means the wire speed and voltage are right.

quiz.q: What does the gas do in MIG welding?
options: Shields the hot metal from air so the weld stays clean
quiz.explain: Shielding gas keeps air away so the weld does not fill with holes.

days.title: MIG Joints
days.goal: Weld butt and corner joints with MIG.
steps: Tack the pieces, check square, then weld.
Use short steady passes, not one long rush.
Let the weld cool between passes on thin metal.
Check the back of the joint for full penetration (the weld reaching through).
days.task: MIG weld a butt joint and a corner joint.
days.challenge: Weld a joint that holds when you bend it.

days.title: MIG vs Stick: Which to Use
days.goal: Know when to use MIG and when to use stick.
steps: MIG is faster and cleaner on thin metal indoors.
Stick works outdoors in wind and on rusty metal.
MIG needs gas and a clean surface.
Choose the right process for each job.
days.task: Pick the right welding process for three different jobs.
days.challenge: Explain MIG vs stick to a friend in plain words.

days.goal: MIG weld a small table frame.

days.task: Finish a MIG-welded table frame, square and strong.
days.challenge: Build the frame with clean welds and no holes.

quiz.q: When is MIG better than stick?
quiz.explain: MIG is fast and clean on thin clean metal indoors.

quiz.q: When is stick better than MIG?
options: Outdoors in wind or on rusty metal
quiz.explain: Stick works in wind and on dirty metal where MIG gas would blow away.

quiz.q: What is full penetration in a weld?
options: The weld reaching right through the joint
quiz.explain: Full penetration means the weld metal reaches through the whole joint.

days.title: Clean Metal Before Welding
days.goal: Clean metal so your welds are strong, not full of holes.
steps: Grind off rust, paint and dirt from the joint area.
Wipe the metal with a clean cloth.
Learn that dirty metal makes weak welds full of holes.
Clean both sides of every joint before you weld.
days.task: Clean a rusty piece until it shines, then weld it.
days.challenge: Tell a clean weld from a dirty one by looking.

days.title: Grinding and Finishing Welds
days.goal: Grind welds smooth and safe to touch.
steps: Wear glasses and gloves when grinding.
Grind the high spots flat with a flap disc.
Round sharp edges so no one gets cut.
Check the finished weld is smooth and strong.
days.task: Grind a weld smooth without thinning the metal.
days.challenge: Finish a weld so it feels smooth to the touch.

days.title: Cut Metal Safely
days.goal: Cut metal straight with a grinder or saw.
steps: Mark the cut line clearly.
Clamp the metal firmly before you cut.
Cut slowly and let the tool do the work.
File the cut edge smooth.
days.task: Cut four bars to exact lengths with clean ends.
days.challenge: Cut a bar square with less than 2mm of error.

quiz.q: Why clean metal before welding?
options: Dirty metal makes weak welds full of holes
quiz.explain: Rust and paint trap gas and weaken the weld.

quiz.q: What should you grind off before welding?
options: Rust, paint and dirt from the joint area
quiz.explain: Only the joint area needs to be clean and shiny for a strong weld.

quiz.q: Why grind welds smooth?
options: So hands do not get cut and the piece looks finished
quiz.explain: Smooth welds are safe to touch and take paint evenly.

quiz.q: Why add a diagonal brace to a gate frame?

capstone.title: Build a Metal Gate, Frame or Furniture Piece
capstone.brief: Design and build a metal gate, frame or furniture piece for a real home, welded, ground smooth and painted, and present it with a costing sheet.
checks: Welds ground smooth and safe to touch
Costing sheet shows metal, rods, gas, time and price
deliverables: Finished metal piece, strong and safe
Four photos: front, side, back and detail
